![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14262782/assets/49c098d7b7fbf15c08d789dc7c2ca2ac4c65ee33c0bfc9bf3d2bed52d4fad608.png)

Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius $1.5,$ as shown above. Find the maximum possible area of the triangle.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $l$ the length of one leg. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is given by

$$
A(l)=\frac{1}{2}l\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}\,.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $3$, the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<3.$

We want to maximize $A(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ 9-{l}^{2}-{l}^{2} & =0 \\ {l}^{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ l & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2})$ | $\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ | $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},3)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $2.5$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Finally, the maximum possible area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{9-{(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Approximate the value of $6\sqrt{87.2}$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)=6\sqrt{x}$ at $x=81.$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $x=a$ is

$$
L(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

In our case, we have $a=81,$ which gives

$$
L(x)=f(81)+{f}^{′}(81)(x-81).
$$

Let's compute $f(81)$ and ${f}^{′}(81)$ in the expression above. Evaluating the function, we get

$$
f(81)=6\sqrt{81}=54,
$$

and computing the derivative, we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\sqrt{x})=\frac{3}{\sqrt{x}},
$$

which in turn gives

$$
{f}^{′}(81)=\frac{3}{\sqrt{81}}=\frac{3}{9}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, the tangent line approximation is

$$
L(x)=54+\frac{1}{3}(x-81).
$$

We can approximate $6\sqrt{87.2}$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=87.2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\sqrt{87.2} & ≈L(87.2) \\  & =54+\frac{1}{3}(87.2-81) \\  & =54+\frac{1}{3}(6.2) \\  & =54+\frac{1}{3}(\frac{31}{5}) \\  & =54+\frac{31}{15} \\  & =\frac{841}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14262782/assets/9283bcc77ac8e63c1ba00f9a81e659bcbcf41bc98b94a1a0617b02feab71cf0a.png)

Car $B$ is being driven due south toward Caltech at a speed of $60\,\text{km/h},$ while car $A$ is being driven due east away from Caltech. When car $B$ is $0.6\,\text{km}$ away from Caltech, car $A$ is $0.8\,\text{km}$ from Caltech. If the distance between the two vehicles is increasing at a rate of $20\,\text{km/h},$ what is the speed of car $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14262782/assets/6e7ef0d4665710a31c1c601048498f20ad6b3099769c1d140320074805964ec7.png)

In the diagram,

- $x$ is the distance between Caltech and car $A$,

- $y$ is the distance between Caltech and car $B$,

- $z$ is the distance between the two cars.

As shown in the diagram, $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ form a right triangle with $z$ as the hypotenuse. We wish to find the rate of change of $x,$ which is $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ 

We know that $x=0.8\,\text{km}$ and $y=0.6\,\text{km}.$ We can find $z$ using the Pythagorean Theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {0.8}^{2}+{0.6}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =1\,\text{km}\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that:

- $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=-60\,\text{km}/\text{h},$

- $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=20\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

Finally, we differentiate both sides of ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={z}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ and then substitute in the known values, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({z}^{2}) \\ 2x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \\ 2(0.8)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(0.6)(-60) & =2(1)(20) \\ 1.6\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =40+72 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{112}{1.6} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =70.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the car $A$ is $70\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=2-{x}^{2}.$ For which of the following values of $k$ does the intermediate value theorem guarantee that $f(x)=k$ has a solution on the interval $x\in [-3,1]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[-3,1],$ so the intermediate value theorem guarantees that $f(x)=k$ has a solution for each value of $k$ between $f(-3)$ and $f(1).$

Since $f(-3)=-7$ and $f(1)=1,$ we must have 
$k\in [-7,1].$

Among the given options, only $k=-2$ belongs to the interval $[-7,1].$

questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosine function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{6})) \\  & =12\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{6})) \\  & =12\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}-1}}\cdot {(\frac{x}{6})}^{′} \\  & =12\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{2}}{36}-1}}\cdot \frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-36}}.\end{aligned}
$$
